Task 7.0: Computational Characterization of molten sulfur TES (M-2.7.1, M-2.7.2, M- 2.7.3, GNG-2D) Computational Fluid Dynamics (CFD) Model Element 16 team established a wide set of numerical simulations to resolve the transient natural convection dynamics of molten sulfur during charge and discharge in a (a) 3D representation of the lab prototype configuration, (b) 2D cross-section slice of the lab prototype configuration and (c) 2D single-tube unit cell domain. Sulfur properties versus temperature were obtained, correlated, and implemented as user defined functions in the computational solver. Figure 35 provides details of the different modeling schemes. Computations using 2D single-tube unit cell domain were first conducted to identify the optimal grid size, time-step size and solver settings based on mesh independent and transient stability studies. Computational simulations using the 3D and 2D cross-sectional domain for the lab prototype were then conducted, which showed that three-dimensional effects along the span of the sulfur TES tank were minimal, and the system dynamics can be characterized using a two-dimensional approach. Figure 35: Computational modeling approaches The final computational setup was based on the 2D-cross section shown in Figure 35 and incorporated the complex temperature-dependent thermophysical properties of sulfur [36-38], as presented in Figure 36. The melting point of sulfur is 118.8°C and the boiling point is 446.6°C at 1 atm [36]. The operational range for the sulfur in the current study is between 120°C to 300°C such that sulfur remains in liquid phase. The viscosity of liquid sulfur is a function of both temperature and the amount of hydrogen sulfide impurities (H S) present in the system [38]. Sulfur forms polymerized chains that rapidly increase 2 the sulfur viscosity by multiple orders of magnitude as temperatures approach 161°C. Above this temperature these chains begin to break apart, leading to orders of magnitude reduction in viscosity. The presence of hydrogen sulfide hinders polymerization, and thus the magnitude of the viscosity variation is strongly dependent on the concentration of impurities. These properties are shown in Figure 36a for pure sulfur along with various concentrations of H S impurities. A major source of uncertainty in the numerical 2 framework is the H S impurity concentration and its impact on the performance due to the 2 change in sulfur viscosity. Hence, the sensitivity of different H S impurity concentrations 2 on model predictions were studied and the results compared against experimental data to identify the sulfur viscosity curve that provides the best agreement with experimental observations.
